title: The Divinity of the Word and the Error of Locality
english: Having left the opinion of the multitude, they decided to seize him through the servants. But no one began against all, being prevented by the divine grace. Being one himself among those who believed, and having been led along with the accusers, he thunders at them, calmly rebuking, showing how they had judged before knowing, if they believed irrationally (John 7:50).

Because they were asking as if he were contained in a human place: 'Where is your father?' (John 8:19), he marvelously said that their not knowing the Father is something they suffer because they also think the Son is nothing other than flesh, the one being seen in a place. And if you know, he says, that even though the Son has borne flesh, he is nothing inferior to the flesh, you would also recognize the Father as not being held by any local containment, but carrying all things in himself.

The evangelist, marveling, appears upon such boldness of speech and such reproofs, with no one being able to lay hold of the Lord, even though they were prepared and ready for this. But nevertheless, teaching in their midst in the temple near the treasury, he was speaking with boldness, providing proofs of divinity, rebuking their ignorance regarding these things, and no one laid hold of him.

To those who will enjoy nothing of his presence, he threatens a painful destruction (John 8:21), and most appropriately; for those from the physician being present only heal, if not receiving [the medicine], those who are dying from their sufferings. And even if it seemed he was refuting himself according to their impious suspicion (John 8:22-23), they were able at any time, being mortals themselves, to go to him; for there is one exit for all, even if the way may seem different and the place receiving all is one before the resurrection of the Lord, even if after these things the order of the saints is transferred into paradise. What then is the Lord? He shows [it] even at their feet, having stated the reason and refuting their suspicion: 'You are of the world' (John 8:22-23). The Word has such a power, that he will be transferred toward himself and toward the heavenly things; therefore this is not death as it is toward a truth, as it would be for a man being of the earth and according to the transfer from the body being drawn under the earth.

Much is, he says, what even God has spoken through the prophets, rebuking your hard-heartedness and disobedience (John 8:26). And I, whatever I speak concerning you, is not from another, but I speak from the Father. And he spoke in a more human and clearer way, reasoning with those listening.

For if they had understood that the Lord was speaking concerning God, they would not have asked, “Where is your father?” (John 8:27); therefore he rightly spoke to them not saying, “You do not know my father.”

He has seen, and while speaking with the Father, he revealed not a sight of the eyes, but a natural knowledge (John 8:38); since he says that even those whom he calls having seen with their Father will not see from anywhere, but rather they are made to belong to the schemes of the evil one by the evilness dwelling in them.

Having foretold that “he who is from God hears the words of God” (John 8:51), he now shows himself to be God by nature; this one keeps the divine commandment, sinning in no way and transgressing the divine acts; this one also hears the divine words. He says that death here is not the fleshly death, which all undergo, but he names as death that which is to come, the punishment for eternity, which is Gehenna and “the worm”; for indeed life is an unending enjoyment for the age, for he says, “the age to come” (John 8:53). Then they say to him, “Do you make yourself greater than Abraham and the prophets, promising to make others greater than them? What are you making of yourself, promising to give less of the zeal from God?”
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Divine Power and the Blind Man
english: It is believed regarding God that no one is the cause of evil. However, the suffering through training and the perception of the power of God working was not fully known later, because of the greater rewards being given to the righteous from God then, and not as now extending the struggles longer because of the life remaining for ages.

Since the blind man was [blind] from birth, it appears to the disciples to seek [the cause]; and as it was impossible for him to commit the same sin before being born, they look to that of the parents. For he knew through the grief of parents that there are sufferings concerning children. But the Lord says that blindness does not come because of some sin, but for the sake of the glory of God about to be, for the purpose of the power of God being known through the paradoxically occurring sight (John 9:7). The participation of Siloam in the work, which is interpreted as having been sent, just as the evangelist did not mark in vain, shows the sending of the Creator's power toward the renewal of his own creation, being made purifying from sins, of which the water of the bath was a symbol, and through the cleansing of sins bringing back health and bringing the diseased and purified nature into perfection.

Not as needing to learn something, these approach the question from the blind man (John 9:10), but as if shaming him with something more defamatory against the Lord because of the perceived brevity regarding the Sabbath (John 9:17); for they thought that being among many, they would drag one down, and these things were meager and cheap, but they thought it great to stop the praise for him and to be able to condemn the thing done not being testified by him who was healed. But he did not show [fear], having known the Lord through trial (John 9:16), but as much as he was able to grasp, he says about him to be a prophet, and this appropriately, since he did not know the authority of the divinity, not knowing that he had made him by his own power.
So much does a pre-conceived dogma and a certain disposition toward the passing of right upon things prevail, and to darken the reasoning.

And that he made the blind man see on the Sabbath, they do not consider; but that 'he made clay' [John 9:6], they judge, being scoffers of the Lord, working his works many times on this day, so that from the 'slavery under the elements' [Galatians 4:3], as the apostle says, he might free the men having made them fit from the Sabbath-slavery into the slavery of God; for to work the work of God according to the Sabbath-rule is to serve God instead of the Sabbath.

Not finding the denial they wanted from the healed one, they seek this from the parents, hoping that they, having been disturbed, would be accomplices to them in denying, because this one born blind is the one now seeing [John 9:18]. But the evangelist says that they do not even believe; for faith does not dwell in a contentious soul and in a soul arraying itself against the power of God, so that they are not without cause for their unbelief, but are even greatly to blame, having constructed hardness within themselves, through which they did not receive the good of faith. They disturb the parents, accusing them, saying that they say their son was born blind; how, they say, to see a son [John 9:28].

You say this out of arrogance. What they say is such a thing. We know that God through Moses gave law, but this one we do not know, except as one loosening the law; for on the Sabbath he healed the blind; for it is for this purpose they say they do not know him [John 9:29-30]. And that you are a disciple of him, they say as if you are disparaging him; and that he does not know, they say as if they are able to conceive nothing concerning the suspicion of his birth according to the flesh, nor anything concerning his unspeakable birth. What then is against this the healed one? From these same words he perceives them and makes them fall upon themselves. This, he says, the wonderful thing, that you do not know where he is from, surpasses human comprehension. Furthermore, since he himself has not spoken from above, but knowing, for he says, 'we know that God does not hear sinners' [John 9:31], that he has spoken.

With a wonderful veil, the parable covers the things revealed to the unworthy, leaving the recognition to the worthy. And the power of the parable is to reveal the departure occurring toward the good from the legal [rule] and...

title: The Shepherd and the Law
english: From the Jewish upbringing to perfection in faith and in following Christ. For the sheep, being well-led by the shepherd, knowing his voice and following him as he leads, are the people of Israel—those who leave behind bodily pursuits and follow the Lord as he exits the world. These are those who understand that truly the things of Christ lead from small things to greater things and not from good to evil, which is the work of not a shepherd, but a thief and a robber, that is, an evil teacher who shifts from law to lawlessness, teaching not to follow him by saying that the sheep should not fall to lawless teachers, those who are obedient to both God and the law.

The shepherd calling his own sheep by name also shows the election of those with [spiritual] pursuits, according to what was said in the prophets: “but you shall gather the sons of Israel one by one”; “for not all have faith.” Nor are all able, since they do not even want to depart from the accustomed habits and be freed from the worldly effort, but to live according to divine discipline and the supra-cosmic, toward which also the Lord guides his own disciples, going before them.

The time for such a parable is most opportune, the present one, teaching about those exiting from the Jewish synagogue; for they indeed brought out those who, having “looked up blind from birth” through the testimony concerning Christ, had been healed. But for him it was not so bad, but the greatest good, because they did not perceive his voice as the cause of the healing. And the one opening the door to the shepherd and opening the entrance decorously is the overseer of Israel, an angel who receives the presence of the king unseemly and hands over to the greater oversight those entrusted to him according to the measure of the domestic commission; for, he says, we were “under stewards” and “deputies” (John 10:6). Proverbs also makes it clear that now he has called the parable (John 10:8).
The Lord entered through the law of fulfillment, being himself in a certain way, and the law; for in the living and true Word, the legal is also contained.

And he led the followers onto pasture and life-giving nourishment, because by the power of the Spirit he feeds them so that they no longer need legal commands, but are led by rational doctrines; for he says, 'having abolished the law of commandments in doctrines' (Galatians 2:19). Indeed, law was given unable to give life, but the Word gives the life of Christ regarding eternal things from the good temporary things, and not life only, but also granting the kingdom within life, which is the abundance.

Who then would be the thieves and robbers who came before the Lord and were not heard by the sheep? And who else but those who taught the law departed through the transfer to the Gentile life, those leading to the alienation of God and bringing destruction through that alienation. Therefore the Lord most necessarily shows a difference from himself from those who transferred from the law, which the apostle also observes by saying: 'For I died by the law according to the law so that I might live to God' (Galatians 2:19); that is, the law was not set aside through lawlessness so that I might be driven into death, but through the truly lawful and divine polity, which leads toward eternal life.

For since false and not good shepherds have stood, shepherds of hire who were for a portion of pleasure, to whom the sheep did not matter, but they were feeding their own pleasure, fleeing from this—the coming of the wolf to the sheep, that is, the destruction that accompanies wickedness—the Lord, so that we might not perish before sin, having taken up such oversight and died to sin for us. But those [shepherds] gave the sheep over to sin, feeding 'themselves' as Ezekiel says (Ezekiel 34:2) and 'not the sheep.' Therefore also God said: 'I will shepherd the sheep' (Ezekiel 34:11) and fulfilled this through the Lord shepherding.

Having said that even the sheep know him (John 10:14), and to this he gave the likeness, saying to the sheep that the knowledge toward him is such as his toward the Father. This indeed is among men the knowledge of the Lord according to virtue, but in the Lord the knowledge of the Father according to nature; for the likeness according to virtue imitates that which is good by nature.
